qs.q: How many bits make up one nibble?
qs.e: A nibble is made up of 4 bits. It is half of a byte.

qs.q: How many bits make up one byte?
qs.e: A byte is made up of 8 bits. It is two nibbles.

qs.q: What mainly determines how an image is represented digitally?

c.x: What the output device is able to display
The size of the file on the hard disk
The programming language used to build it
The brand of the monitor showing the image

qs.e: Image representation depends on what the output device can display. Example: a seven-segment display needs only 7 bits.

qs.q: How many bits are used to represent each pixel in a binary (monochrome) image?
qs.e: A binary image represents each pixel using a <mark>single bit</mark>.

qs.q: Why is a binary image also called a monochrome image?

c.x: Because it contains no color information at all
Because it is always displayed in a blue tint
Because it requires no storage space to save
Because it is always compressed before saving

qs.e: A binary image is a 1-bit monochrome image. It contains no color, only black or white per pixel.

qs.q: How many bits are used to represent each pixel in a grayscale image?
qs.e: A grayscale image represents each pixel using 8 bits. These 8 bits are stored as one byte.

qs.q: What is the value range of a single pixel in an 8-bit grayscale image?
e: Each pixel uses 8 bits, so it can take 28 = 256 different values.
Counting starts from 0, so the values run from 0 to 255.
Result: 0 to 255

qs.q: How many bits are used to represent each pixel in a 24-bit color image?
qs.e: A color image represents each pixel using <mark>24 bits</mark>.

qs.q: Which three color components together make up each pixel in a 24-bit color image?
qs.e:
Each pixel in a 24-bit color image is composed of three values:
<mark>Red, Green, and Blue</mark> (RGB).

qs.q: How many distinct colors can a 24-bit color image represent in total?
e: Each pixel has three components: Red, Green, and Blue.
Each component has 256 possible values.
Total colors = 256 x 256 x 256 = 2<sup>24</sup>.
Result: 16,777,216 possible colors.

qs.q: Which two properties are used to characterize a simple sound wave?
qs.e:
A simple sound wave can be characterized by its:
<mark>amplitude</mark> and <mark>frequency</mark>.

qs.q: What happens to a sound as its amplitude increases?
qs.e: The larger the amplitude, the louder the sound.

qs.q: What happens to a sound's tone as its frequency increases?
qs.e: The higher the frequency, the higher the tone.

qs.q: What is the process called in which the voltage of a sound wave is measured at frequent intervals?
qs.e: <mark>Sampling</mark> is the process of measuring the voltage of a sound wave at frequent intervals.

qs.q: What is the process called in which sampled sound values are stored as a binary code?
qs.e: <mark>Decoding</mark> is the process of storing the sampled values as a binary code.

qs.q: What is a typical sampling rate mentioned for digitizing a sound wave?
qs.e: The voltage is typically sampled at <mark>48 kHz</mark> per second when digitizing sound.

qs.q: How many bits per sample are typically used when decoding a digitized sound wave?
qs.e: Decoding typically stores each sample as a binary code of <mark>16 or 32 bits</mark>.

qs.q: What is each individual image in a video sequence called?
qs.e: A video is composed of a sequence of continuous images. Each image is called a frame.

qs.q: Roughly how fast must frames be displayed for a video to appear as continuous movement?
qs.e:
Each frame is flashed on the screen for a short time.
When frames are displayed <mark>faster than 50 per second</mark>, they create the impression of continuous movement.

qs.q: Why is a standard code needed for representing characters digitally?

c.x: To ensure the same code is used on every computer
To automatically make every file smaller
To allow only a single language to be typed
To increase the processing speed of the CPU

qs.e: A standard is needed to ensure that the code used on your computer is the same as the code used on any other computer.

qs.q: What does the abbreviation ASCII stand for?

c.x: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
Advanced System Code for Information Interchange
American Standard Code for Internal Indexing
Automated Symbol Coding for Information Input

qs.e: ASCII stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange.

qs.q: What does the abbreviation EBCDIC stand for?

c.x: Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code
Enhanced Binary Character Data Input Code
External Byte Coded Decimal Indexing Code

qs.e: EBCDIC stands for Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code.

qs.q: Which company historically used the EBCDIC code on its mainframe computers?
qs.e: EBCDIC was used in the past by <mark>IBM</mark> mainframes.

qs.q: Why can't ASCII or EBCDIC represent character sets such as Chinese, Arabic, or Japanese?

c.x: They are limited to only 256 possible combinations
These languages have no written characters at all
These codes only support numbers, not letters
These languages require sound instead of text

qs.e: ASCII and EBCDIC are limited to 256 possible combinations. So character sets like Chinese, Arabic, and Japanese cannot be represented using them.

qs.q: How many bytes does Unicode use to represent each character?
qs.e: Unicode uses <mark>2 bytes</mark> for each character.

qs.q: What is the main disadvantage of Unicode compared to single-byte codes like ASCII?

c.x: It takes twice as much space to store characters
It cannot represent any special symbols at all
It only supports English letters and digits
It requires an internet connection to render

qs.e: Unicode takes <mark>twice as much space</mark> to store the same number of characters as a single-byte code.

qs.q: Represent the following code in UTF-8. Separate the bytes in your answer with a space. `1110 0111 01 011011 101011`
e: Join the groups into one code: `1110011101011011101011` (22 bits).
Choose the template. A 4-byte template holds only 3 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 21 data bits, so a 5-byte template is needed: `111110xx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx` (2 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 26 data bits).
Fill the x positions starting from the right-most bit: Last byte: `101011` Previous byte: `011011` Previous byte: `011101`
Only 4 bits remain (`1110`) for the second byte, so pad 0s on the left: `001110`. The first byte gets the remaining x bits `00`.
Look at the first byte: `110xxxxx` starts with two 1s, so the character is made of exactly 2 bytes.
A 2-byte character is this first byte followed by only one continuation byte (`10xxxxxx`), which is the second byte `10000000`.
The third byte `10000000` is a continuation byte that belongs to no first byte. Result: the sequence is not a correct UTF-8 code.

qs.q: Encode the Unicode code point `U+1F603` using UTF-8. Which byte sequence is the result?
e: The code point value is `1F603` in hexadecimal. Convert to binary: `0001 1111 0110 0000 0011` (17 significant bits: `11111011000000011`).
Choose the template. The value is above U+FFFF (up to U+1FFFFF), so a 4-byte template is needed: `11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx` (3 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 21 data bits).
Fill the x positions from the right-most bit: Last byte: `000011` Third byte: `011000` Second byte: `011111`
Only 3 bits remain for the first byte (`000`), so it is `11110000`. The unused x positions are padded with 0s on the left.

qs.q: Represent the following 8-bit code in UTF-32. Write the bytes with the MSB on the left, separated by a space. `01000000`
e: UTF-32 encodes every character on exactly <mark>4 bytes</mark>, "as it is".
The code has 8 bits (1 byte), so 3 bytes of zeros must be added.
With the MSB on the left, the zero bytes go on the left. Result: `00000000 00000000 00000000 01000000`

qs.q: Represent the following 17-bit code in UTF-32. Write the bytes with the MSB on the left, separated by a space. If it is impossible, choose x. `1 00000000 11111111`
e: UTF-32 stores a character on exactly 4 bytes (32 bits). 17 bits fit inside 32 bits, so it is possible.
Split the 17 bits from the right into bytes: `11111111` (last byte), `00000000` (second-to-last byte), and `1` (remaining bit).
Pad the remaining bit to a full byte: `00000001`.
Add one more byte of zeros on the left to reach 4 bytes: `00000000`.

qs.q: Represent the following 32-bit code in UTF-32. Write the bytes with the MSB on the left, separated by a space. If it is impossible, choose x. `01111111 11111111 11111111 11111111`
e: UTF-32 encodes a character on exactly <mark>4 bytes</mark>, "as it is".
The code already has 32 bits (4 bytes), so no padding is needed and nothing changes.
Result (MSB on the left): the same as the input, `01111111 11111111 11111111 11111111`

qs.q: A 64-bit word with the hexadecimal value `1122334455667788` is stored at address 9656 (decimal) in the memory of a little-endian computer with 8-bit bytes. What is the address of the byte containing the value `22`?
e: Divide the hexadecimal value into bytes: `11 22 33 44 55 66 77 88`.

A little-endian computer stores the <mark>LSB first</mark>, at the lowest address, so the arrangement is:
`88 77 66 55 44 33 22 11`
Assign addresses starting from 9656: 88 at 9656, 77 at 9657, 66 at 9658, 55 at 9659, 44 at 9660, 33 at 9661, 22 at 9662, 11 at 9663.
Result: the byte containing `22` is at address 9662.

qs.q: In a UTF-8 multi-byte character, which part tells the decoder how many bytes the character occupies?

c.x: The run of trailing 0 bits in the last byte
A separate length field placed before the character
The first two bits of the last byte
The run of leading 1 bits in the first byte

qs.e: The first byte works as a counter: `110xxxxx` means 2 bytes, `1110xxxx` means 3 bytes, `11110xxx` means 4 bytes, and so on. Every byte after the first starts with `10`, so it carries no length information.

qs.q: A byte inside a UTF-8 stream begins with the bits `10`. What does this tell the decoder?

c.x: It marks the end of the whole text
It is the first byte of a two-byte character
It is an ASCII character stored in one byte

qs.e: In a multi-byte UTF-8 encoding, every byte after the first one starts with `10`, so such a byte is a continuation byte. A first byte starts with `0` (one-byte character) or with two or more 1s (multi-byte character).

qs.q: The first byte of a UTF-8 character is `11110xxx`. How many bytes does the whole character occupy?
e: Count the leading 1s of the first byte: `11110xxx` starts with four 1s.
The number of leading 1s equals the total number of bytes. Result: 4 bytes = the first byte + 3 continuation bytes (`10xxxxxx`).

qs.q: How many bits are available to hold the code point (the x positions) in a 3-byte UTF-8 character?
e: The 3-byte template is `1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx`.
First byte: `1110` uses 4 of its 8 bits, leaving 4 x positions.
Each continuation byte: `10` uses 2 of its 8 bits, leaving 6 x positions: 6 + 6 = 12.
Total: 4 + 12 = 16 bits. The other 8 bits (`1110`, `10`, `10`) are control bits.

qs.q: Which of the following byte sequences is a valid UTF-8 encoding of a single character?
e: Use the first byte to find the length: a first byte starting with `110` means 2 bytes in total, so exactly one continuation byte starting with `10` must follow.
`11010101 10000011`: first byte starts with `110`, second starts with `10` → <mark>valid</mark>.
`11010101 11000011`: the second byte starts with `11`, not `10` → invalid.
`10010101 10000011`: the first byte starts with `10`, a continuation pattern that cannot start a character → invalid.
`11010101 10000011 10000011`: after the one required continuation byte there is an extra `10xxxxxx` byte that belongs to no first byte → invalid.

qs.q: Why is UTF-32 not compatible with ASCII?

c.x: Each ASCII character takes 8 bytes instead of 1
UTF-32 gives new numbers to ASCII characters
Each ASCII character takes 4 bytes instead of 1

qs.e: UTF-32 stores every character, including those in the ASCII range, on a full 4-byte unit, whereas ASCII uses one byte per character. Because of the different byte layout, ASCII data cannot be read as UTF-32, and the reverse is also true.

qs.q: Which problem comes from the fact that UTF-32 stores each character "as it is" on 4 bytes?

c.x: Characters cannot be counted without scanning the text
Characters below 128 cannot be stored at all
The order of the 4 bytes (endianness) is ambiguous
Characters need a first byte that marks the length

qs.e: The 4 bytes of a character can be written with the MSB first or with the LSB first. The same character therefore has two possible byte sequences, and the receiver must know which byte order was used (endianness).

qs.q: Which of the following is an advantage of UTF-32 compared with variable-length encodings such as UTF-8?

c.x: Less storage space needed for English text files
No byte-order problems when exchanging data between machines
Faster operations such as counting characters
Compatibility with existing ASCII files and tools

qs.e: In UTF-32 every character has the same size (4 bytes), so operations such as counting characters or jumping to the n-th character are simple. The cost: it is very wasteful in space, it is not ASCII compatible, and it has the endianness problem.

qs.q: Why is UTF-32 problematic in systems that expect null-terminated strings?

c.x: Its characters have no marker showing where each character ends
It stores every character with a variable number of bytes in total
It cannot encode the null character in any form at all
Zero bytes inside characters look like the string end

qs.e:
A null-terminated string ends at the first byte equal to `00000000`.
In UTF-32 many characters contain such <mark>zero bytes</mark> (for example the upper bytes of any small code point), so a program may think the string ended <u>in the middle</u> of a character.

qs.q: In the 4-byte value below, written with the most-significant byte on the left, which byte is the LSB (least-significant byte)? `10101001 01001010 10101011 10001100`
qs.e: The LSB is the byte with the lowest significance, which is the right-most byte: `10001100`. The MSB is the left-most byte: `10101001`.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes big-endian from little-endian when a multi-byte value is stored in memory? "First" means at the lowest address.

c.x: Big-endian stores the MSB first and little-endian stores the LSB first
Big-endian is used for 64-bit words and little-endian for 32-bit words
Big-endian stores the LSB first and little-endian stores the MSB first
Big-endian reverses the bits inside each byte and little-endian does not

qs.e: Big-endian: the most-significant byte (MSB) is stored first, at the lowest address. Little-endian: the least-significant byte (LSB) is stored first, at the lowest address. Neither order is superior to the other.

qs.q: The 32-bit hexadecimal value `12345678` is stored at address 100, and then <u>only the single byte</u> at address 100 is loaded. What is the loaded byte?

c.x: `78` on both a big-endian and a little-endian machine
`12` on a big-endian machine and `78` on a little-endian machine
`78` on a big-endian machine and `12` on a little-endian machine
`12` on both a big-endian and a little-endian machine

e: Divide the value into bytes: `12 34 56 78`.
Big-endian stores the MSB first: address 100 holds `12`, 101 holds `34`, 102 holds `56`, 103 holds `78`.
Little-endian stores the LSB first: address 100 holds `78`, 101 holds `56`, 102 holds `34`, 103 holds `12`.

Result: loading the byte at address 100 gives `12` on a big-endian machine and `78` on a little-endian machine. This is why endianness matters when a multi-byte value is stored and then only a subset of its bytes is loaded.

qs.q: In which situation must a programmer account for endianness?

c.x: Comparing two values of the same size inside one machine's memory
Sending multi-byte data from a big-endian to a little-endian machine
Storing a single byte in memory and then loading the same byte back again
Adding two whole integers that are already held in the processor registers

qs.e: Endianness matters when a multi-byte value is stored to memory and a subset of its bytes is loaded, or when such data is sent between machines with different byte orders (for example big-endian to little-endian). A single byte has no byte order, and operations inside one machine on whole values are not affected.
